# Microsoft Windows Server Resilient File System (ReFS) NTFS alternative.
## Channel: ITSystemsAdmin
18.8K subscribers
2 likes

### Description
307 views
Posted: 2026-02-23
Microsoft Windows Server 2025 utilizes the Resilient File System (ReFS) to maximize data availability, integrity, and scalability, offering a modern alternative to NTFS for high-performance, large-scale storage. Key features in 2025 include improved NVMe performance, enhanced deduplication and compression, and auto-repairing capabilities, making it ideal for VMs and Storage Spaces Direct. 

|| Key Features of ReFS in Windows Server 2025
__Data Integrity and Self-Healing: ReFS uses checksums to detect corruption and automatically repairs data (especially when used with Storage Spaces) without taking the volume offline. [...] __Performance Improvements: ReFS in 2025 is optimized for NVMe and NVMe over Fabrics, providing faster performance for large-scale data storage, such as Hyper-V virtual machines.

__Advanced Deduplication & Compression: A rebuilt deduplication engine (using Set-ReFsDedup cmdlets) offers significant storage savings for high-performance workloads.

__Scalability: ReFS supports vastly larger file sizes and volumes (up to 35 PB) compared to NTFS.

__Confidential VM Support: Windows Server 2025 enables booting directly from ReFS-formatted drives for enhanced security in confidential virtual machines.

__New "DevDrive" Capability: ReFS can be used for "DevDrive," optimized for developer scenarios to improve performance. [...] || Considerations
__Performance Issues (Potential): Some reports indicate potential high CPU/RAM utilization with ReFS in certain 2025 builds, necessitating careful monitoring.

__Use Cases: ReFS is ideal for virtual machine storage, Veeam repositories, and large-scale data storage (Storage Spaces Direct), but it is not intended as a replacement for NTFS on system boot drives for general servers.

__Limitations: ReFS does not support all legacy NTFS features, such as file-level encryption.

"Its primary use case is on file servers that store extremely large amounts of data. It has data integrity and recovery mechanisms built into the file system, as well. That means those tools that are designed to detect and repair file corruption in other file systems aren’t necessary, so their incompatibility with ReFS isn’t really an issue. "

ReFS is NTFS’s little brother. Its used more for data storage than anything else. Once it grows up I can see it replacing NTFS. But this might not happen for many years as there are lots of NTFS features it doesn’t support currently.

Yeah, currently it’s not promoted as a replacement, rather something new for a particular need (Hyper-V, file server, backup storage). They both now (ReFS and NTFS) should co-exist not compete. [...] It’s obvious that ReFS in its current iteration is not a replacement for NTFS, but rather is intended for use in specific circumstances, particularly for storage of very large data sets. The different underlying structure and lack of support for some of the features that we’ve come to take for granted in NTFS present a “gotcha” for anyone who would aspire to use ReFS as the main file system, because some applications that rely on specific NTFS features might not work with ReFS. Many NTFS disk tools don’t work with ReFS, either, because it handles the file metadata differently.

# Resilient File System (ReFS) overview

## In this article

The Resilient File System (ReFS) is a modern file system developed by Microsoft to maximize data availability, scale efficiently to large data sets across diverse workloads, and provide data integrity with resiliency to corruption. ReFS seeks to address an expanding set of storage scenarios and establish a foundation for future innovations. [...] For Windows Server deployments, mirror-accelerated parity is only supported on Storage Spaces Direct. We recommend using mirror-accelerated parity with archival and backup workloads only. For virtualized and other high performance random workloads, we recommend using three-way mirrors for better performance.

Accelerated VM operations - ReFS improves the performance of virtualized workloads:

Variable cluster sizes - ReFS supports both 4K and 64K cluster sizes. 4K is the recommended cluster size for most deployments, but 64K clusters are appropriate for large, sequential IO workloads.

### Scalability

ReFS is designed to support extremely large data sets - millions of terabytes - without negatively impacting performance, achieving greater scale than prior file systems. [...] This overview explains how ReFS helps protect data from corruption, supports large-scale storage environments, and integrates with key Windows Server technologies. Use this guide to understand ReFS benefits, deployment scenarios, and feature comparisons with NTFS.

## Key benefits

Learn about the key benefits that ReFS provides, including: resiliency, performance, and scalability.

### Resiliency

ReFS has features that can precisely detect corruptions and also fix those corruptions while remaining online, helping provide increased integrity and availability for your data:
